title: Only 10% Of The Population Can Pass This Grammar Quiz
summary: Sentence structure, verbs, punctuation and almost-correct wording collide in one fast proofreading challenge.

landing.intro: Think your grammar is flawless? Repair broken sentences, catch tiny punctuation traps and prove you can spot the mistake before it catches you.

startPrompt.title: Proofreading Test Ready ✍️
startPrompt.copy: Watch a short ad to start the test.

about.body:
This worldwide grammar quiz condenses practical editing into one focused ten-question challenge. It covers sentence structure, verb forms, punctuation, pronoun clarity, modifier placement and the judgement needed to improve real notices and short documents.

The challenge tests grammar shared across major standard-English varieties. It avoids spelling differences, optional punctuation styles, dialect traps and constructions where respected authorities accept more than one form, so every scored answer follows from the wording and register shown on screen.

Your final percentage reflects only the answers selected in this entertainment challenge. It is a playful snapshot of the language patterns you recognised most confidently, not a formal measure of English proficiency, education or professional editing ability.

howToPlay.title: How to Play
steps: Answer ten varied proofreading questions and choose the single option best supported by the sentence or document shown.
Correct answers stay hidden while you play, so inspect every verb, reference and punctuation mark before the test moves on.
Finish the challenge to reveal your Grammar Score, strongest skill and complete result report.

about.disclaimer: For entertainment and general learning only. This quiz is not a formal English-language assessment, academic qualification or proof of language proficiency.

profiles.title: The Master Editor
profiles.copy: You handled structure, reference and tiny punctuation details with exceptional control. Even the final multi-clue edits rarely disturbed your command of the page.

profiles.title: The Natural Grammarian
profiles.copy: You recognised how sentences fit together and caught most of the challenge’s nearly invisible errors. Your judgement stayed reliable as the material moved from isolated lines to real editing contexts.

profiles.title: The Sentence Specialist
profiles.copy: You solved a strong majority of the proofreading problems and adapted well when the format changed. A few fine distinctions kept the final result interesting.

profiles.title: The Careful Communicator
profiles.copy: You have a dependable grasp of everyday grammar and a clear eye for several important editing patterns. Your strongest skill shows where that language instinct becomes most confident.

profiles.title: The Language Improver
profiles.copy: You caught a solid share of the errors and kept adjusting as the challenge became more demanding. The review will show which patterns are ready to become second nature.

profiles.title: The Grammar Detective
profiles.copy: The challenge found some well-hidden traps, but it also revealed the language clues you already notice naturally. Every missed answer is a useful pattern to recognise next time.

insights.overview: Your grammar score at a glance

details.analysisTitle: How to read your grammar score
details.analysisCopy: This ten-question result combines sentence structure, agreement, punctuation, reference, modifier placement and editing judgement. Each answer moves the percentage by ten points, so the skill pattern below adds useful context to the headline score.
details.roadmapIntro: Your score is only the opening line. Continue through the report to see which language patterns held strongest and which details created the hardest traps.
details.positionCopy: The challenge target is eight correct answers out of ten. Your marker shows how close this attempt came to that entertainment-only pass line.
details.measuredIntro: The questions deliberately mix three broad forms of language judgement instead of repeating a single textbook rule.

measuredAreas.title: Structure and agreement
measuredAreas.copy: Connecting clauses clearly and keeping verb forms aligned with the meaning and timeline shown.

measuredAreas.title: Punctuation and reference
measuredAreas.copy: Using marks and pronouns to make relationships precise without relying on optional house style.

measuredAreas.title: Editing for meaning
measuredAreas.copy: Preserving the intended scope, emphasis and register while repairing realistic documents.

details.tipsTitle: Three ways to sharpen your editing eye
details.tipsIntro: These are simple practice ideas for a future attempt—not a formal language assessment.

tips.title: Read for meaning first
tips.copy: Decide exactly what the sentence must communicate before comparing its punctuation or word order.

tips.title: Find the sentence core
tips.copy: Identify the main subject and verb, then check whether every added phrase attaches clearly.

tips.title: Return to the near misses
tips.copy: Review why a plausible distractor changes emphasis, reference or agreement before trying again.

questions.question: Although the rain stopped ___ the path remained slippery. What belongs in the gap?
questions.explanation: A comma follows the introductory dependent clause before the complete main clause begins.

questions.question: Which sentence has correct subject–verb agreement?
answers: The list of ingredients are on the counter.
The list of ingredients is on the counter.
The list of ingredients were on the counter.
The list of ingredients be on the counter.
questions.explanation: The singular subject is “list,” so it takes the singular verb “is.”

questions.question: The meeting began at 09:00. Leo finished the chart at 08:30. Which sentence is correct?
answers: Leo completes the chart before the meeting began.
Leo was completing the chart after the meeting begins.
Leo has completed the chart after the meeting began.
Leo had completed the chart before the meeting began.
questions.explanation: The past perfect marks the earlier completed action, while the simple past marks the later meeting.

questions.question: Which sentence uses a semicolon correctly?
answers: The file; because it was large, loaded slowly.
The file was large; it loaded slowly.
The file was; large and loaded slowly.
The file was large; and because loaded slowly.
questions.explanation: A semicolon correctly joins the two closely related independent clauses.

questions.question: Which sentence uses the object pronoun correctly?
answers: Please send the draft to Lina and me.
Please send the draft to Lina and I.
Please send the draft to she and me.
Please send the draft to Lina and myself.
questions.explanation: After the preposition “to,” the object pronoun “me” is required.

questions.question: Several chefs share these lockers. Which sign is written correctly?
answers: The chefs lockers
The chef's lockers
The chefs' lockers
The chefs's lockers
questions.explanation: The apostrophe follows the plural noun “chefs” to show that the lockers belong to several chefs.

questions.question: Which notice is grammatically correct?
answers: Visitors must signing in, wear a badge and return it.
Visitors must sign in, wear a badge and return it before leaving.
Visitors must signed in, wear a badge and returning it.
Visitors signing in, badge wearing and it returns.
questions.explanation: “Sign,” “wear” and “return” use matching base forms after “must.”

questions.question: Only the first report was revised. Which sentence makes that meaning unambiguous?
answers: Only the editor revised the first report.
The editor revised the first report only to correct the title.
The editor revised the first report only yesterday.
The editor revised only the first report.
trapdoorErrors: only changes who performed the action
the purpose phrase changes why the report was revised
only changes when the action happened
questions.explanation: Placing “only” immediately before “the first report” restricts the revision to that report.

questions.question: Which numbered part contains the error?

visual.ariaLabel: The final reports were checked before the editor approve them

answers: A
B
C
D
questions.explanation: Part C needs the past-tense verb “approved” to match the completed action.

questions.question: Which sentence is completely correct?
answers: After reviewing the figures, Maya confirmed that each total was accurate.
After reviewing the figures, each total were confirmed by Maya.
After reviewing the figures Maya confirmed, that each total was accurate.
After reviewing the figures; Maya confirmed that each total were accurate.
questions.explanation: The opening modifier clearly describes Maya, the comma is correctly placed and “each total” takes the singular verb “was.”
